title: Sancho Panza Governs Barataria
text:
In the second part of Don Quixote, a duke and duchess entertain themselves by making Sancho Panza, Don Quixote's simple, illiterate squire, governor of an "island" called Barataria, really a town on their estate. They expect him to make a fool of himself.

He surprises everyone. In one case, an old man swore he had repaid a debt of ten gold crowns, handing his walking stick to the lender to hold while he took the oath. Sancho noticed the stick, had it broken open, and found the ten crowns inside. In another, a woman accused a herdsman of assault and was awarded his purse, and when he tried to take it back from her she fought him off with such strength that Sancho concluded she could easily have defended herself the first time, and gave the purse back. He issued sensible ordinances on prices, wine and beggars.

The pranks did not stop. A court doctor took away every dish before Sancho could eat it, and on the seventh night of his rule he was woken by a staged invasion, strapped between two shields and trampled. The next morning he went to the stable, embraced his donkey, and resigned. He had come into the governorship without a penny, he said, and he was leaving without one, which few governors could say.
lesson: Good judgment often comes from paying attention, common sense and honesty more than from rank or education. And knowing when to walk away from a position is part of handling it well.
people: Sancho Panza, the Duke and Duchess, Doctor Pedro Recio
source: Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part II, Chapters 45 to 53
